title: the summit sit
hook: a checkup that ends with 'you're fine', and an old definition of health that doesn't stop at the body

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to the Vedas, and Ushas, the dawn who wakes every living thing. Did you catch a minute of morning light before a screen? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `THE DAWN, BEFORE THE SCREEN.`

segments.voice: The paper gown, the cold stethoscope, the blood pressure cuff that squeezes a little too long. At the end, the doctor glances at the chart and says: you're fine. And that's good news. But you're fine, there, mostly means nothing is wrong. Something missing, something broken: none found. Months back, this path spent a stretch with a classical tradition that asked a different question. Not what's wrong with you, but what does it look like when you're well? Today's summit sit climbs back to Ayurveda, read as a lens, and to the breath.
screen: `A COLD STETHOSCOPE.` → `YOU'RE FINE.` → `WHAT DOES WELL LOOK LIKE?`

segments.voice: First, what the year was careful to say. Ayurveda here was a way of noticing, not a diagnosis, and nothing in it replaces a doctor. With that said, look back. The doshas, vata, pitta and kapha, were read like weather: dry and moving, hot and sharp, heavy and steady, words for noticing how a day or a body feels. The Charaka Samhita's daily round started before dawn, cleaned the teeth and the tongue, oiled the body like a new cricket bat, and said to exercise only to half your strength. It also told you to greet people first. Charaka named supports of life, and food and sleep were two of them. Then the breath, with every claim checked: Patanjali asks for breath that is long and subtle, not forced. Now the summit view. One classical definition of the healthy person, in the Sushruta Samhita, lists the body in balance: its doshas, its digestive fire, its tissues, its wastes. And then, in paraphrase, it doesn't stop there. It ends with a self, senses and mind that are clear and content. Health, in that definition, reaches all the way to whether the mind is at ease. That's why it fit on a path like this one. And it fits the end of this week, too. This week the summit sits went back through the Rudram, the schools of thought, karma and seva, bhakti, jnana, the Vedas, and now this. Different languages for the same climb: a person trying to live well, inside and out.
screen: `A WAY OF NOTICING, NOT A DIAGNOSIS.` · `THE DAILY ROUND: HALF YOUR STRENGTH.` · `BREATH, LONG AND SUBTLE.` · `HEALTH ENDS WITH A MIND AT EASE.` · then, large: `WELL, NOT JUST NOT SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: Patanjali's breath. Sit comfortably, and don't change anything at first. Just notice the breath as it is. Then, without forcing, let the out-breath grow a little longer, and a little quieter. Long and subtle, not big and loud. If it strains, let it go back to normal. Then, at the end of the sit, ask the old question, gently: are the senses at ease? Is the mind content, even a little? Don't fix anything. Just notice. The bell holds the time.

The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: Ayurveda as a lens, the breath made long and subtle, and a definition of health that ends with a mind at ease. Today's word.

Your line: the summit sit. Today, once, ask yourself not what's wrong, but what well would look like right now, and do one small thing toward it. A week on the summit, done. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some Hindus draw on Ayurvedic ideas in daily life, through a morning routine, seasonal eating, or attention to sleep, alongside modern medicine; people who practice yoga often work with slow, unforced breathing.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: svastha, healthy, the word for the well person in the classical definition.

trapdoor: what you thought: health means nothing is wrong.
what it means: in one classical definition, it means a body in balance and a mind at ease.

sources.ref: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 5, 7 and 8 (daily routine; exercise to half strength; greeting first); 11 (the supports of life)

notes: Summit sit, day 10: revisits 'Ayurveda as a lens' (1286–1320) and 'the breath again — every claim checked' (1321–1327). Week end (week of 1415–1421), so the teach and carry look back over the week's summit sits.
Health framing: the script repeats that Ayurveda is offered as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis, and does not replace a doctor. No health claims are made.
Sushruta Samhita Sutrasthana 15 (often cited as 15.41 or 15.48 depending on edition): samadosha, samagni, samadhatu-malakriya, prasanna-atma-indriya-manah, svastha. Confirm reference and paraphrase.

Charaka: daily routine (Sutrasthana 5), exercise to half strength (Sutrasthana 7), the supports of life including food and sleep (Sutrasthana 11). The voice avoids stating how many supports. The cricket-bat image and 'greet people first' are recalled from 1296 and 1298. Confirm.
Women of the epics and the regional traditions remain for the summit sits of 1422–1424 (another writer).
Editor pass: the 'legs of a stool' image cut (1402 used legs of a cot); Charaka Sutrasthana 8 added for 'greet people first'.
